newsitem.title: USA: Republicans see China funds as serious matter.
newsitem.headline: Republicans see China funds as serious matter.

text.p: Republican lawmakers on Saturday voiced serious concern about new allegations that the Chinese government may have given money to the Democratic Party for the 1996 presidential election campaign.
U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms said his committee would investigate the allegations and question administration officials about the matter.

"The United States has no alternative but to follow this lead all the way to the end, and we're going to do it on the Foreign Relations Committee, I assure you of that," Helms told CNN's "Evans & Novak" program in an interview taped on Friday.

Rep. Bob Livingston, chairman of the House Appropriations Committee, said the latest allegations, published in a Washington Post report on Thursday, compounded his concerns about campaign finance abuses by the Clinton administration.

"There are three relevations a day, before breakfast, about this White House," the Louisiana Republican told CNN's "Capital Gang." "There is a suggested pallor of corruption that is out there that gains credence every single day -- and if it's not corruption, it sure as hell is bad judgment."
President Bill Clinton on Thursday backed a "thorough" investigation into the allegations, saying he had no knowledge of the charges, but said "they obviously have to be thoroughly investigated."
It is illegal for a foreign government or foreigners in most cases to donate to U.S. campaigns.

White House Counsel Lanny Davis told CNN's "Inside Politics" the president viewed the allegations as very serious. "If they turn out to be true, then he certainly would favor full law enforcement in this matter," Davis said.

Rep. David McIntosh called the Post report "a serious matter", saying it raised the specter of "a huge secret web where the government was used to raise money for campaign purposes from China, from people in the United States."

McIntosh, whose House subcommittee is investigating the alleged use of a White House database for campaign purposes, said the Clinton administration had been less than forthcoming in complying with the panel's requests for information.

Documents released to the committee were heavily censored, making it difficult to "tell what was happening, who was involved, and to what extent it was being used for politics," the Indiana Republican told CNN's "Inside Politics."

The White House has denied that its computerized database had been used to raise money for Clinton's re-election campaign or for any other unauthorized purposes, including controversial overnight stays in the Lincoln bedroom.
McIntosh warned that his subcommittee was ready to ask for a congressional subpoena if the White House did not send unedited records to Capitol Hill soon.

Davis said McIntosh and his staff had been given unlimited access to the documents in question at the White House. Some materials released to the subcommittee for public disclosure had been edited to protect the privacy of the Clintons and guests who stayed at the White House, Davis said.
This included the names of personal friends of the Clintons who stayed overnight at the White House, Social Security numbers and unlisted telephone numbers.
"There's an aspect of privacy that every president and first lady are entitled to," he said.
